title: Chapter 10: Reverse Order
blurb: Fintan crosses alone to win his name back and finds it has already travelled somewhere he cannot follow.

blocks.text: The Ninefold at dawn has nobody in it who is paid to be there. The lamps were down to their last inch. Nine doors stood in their walls, doing nothing, which is what doors do until somebody tells them where to go.
I stood in the east wall's third door with the Bole packet under my arm, my own route on my tongue, and nobody counting for me.
I said the route. It is one hinge long. It has my mother in it.
The cold went out of the stone under my hand.
"Nine," I said, out loud, to nobody. "Eight."
I stepped through.
Footnote: Brisk says talking to doors is normal. Brisk also says she's thirty-six.
The letter had said come now. I came on day eighty-six. That is six days late, and I can account for every one of them.

The Bole's side of the Weirside pair opens once a day, and the Exchange Desk spends that opening every dawn, handing the packet through. A Chainman who wants it must carry the packet himself, by hand, and the Desk keeps a rota for that. My name came up for day eighty-six.
I could have asked to jump the rota. I didn't ask. Come alone is not a phrase people use when the news is good, and I was in no hurry to hear the rest of it.
I was also frightened. That isn't on any form, but it accounts for the six days better than the rota does, and I'd like it noted.
On the afternoon of day eighty-five Brisk found me in the threshold room, a pace back from the east wall's third door, moving my lips.
"Talking to her?"
"Practising. From outside the frame." A route read by someone who isn't standing in the doorway opens nothing. I had checked that clause twice before I tried it.
"Talking to doors is normal," Brisk said. "I do it all the time. She likes it."
"How old are you, Brisk?"
"Thirty-six."
"On day eighty you were twenty-seven."
"Grew up fast." She looked at the door, and then at me, and she didn't ask where I was going. "Count out loud, Ardent. Nobody counts right in their head."

That night I made my ballast at home, after my mother had gone up, with my door shut and the lamp turned to the wall. One piece, of a kind I have never spent at Weirside. I have spent one kind there, on day forty-two. This would be the second. I made a spare of a different kind in case something spoiled the first. I won't describe either. Describing it is half of telling it.
Footnote: ballast settles at the seventh midnight after it's made. Day ninety-two. If I wasn't home by then, ballast would be the least of it.

I wrote my Form 9 at the kitchen table in pinned ink. Four lines, the same four as day eighty. My given name is Edric. I write shorthand at ninety words a minute. My father is Tobin Ardent. I remember my father's voice. Behind it in the folder I put my bill from day nought, whose first line reads false.
My mother came down for a glass of water and saw the folder.
"Work?"
"Packet run tomorrow. Home by dark."
"Mind the weir path, Edric."
I said I would. I have not told her where the packet goes, or who lives at the other end of it. That is a separate matter, and I am keeping it separate.

Before dawn I signed the Ninefold's threshold log, in ordinary ink, because that is what it takes: Ardent, E. Chainman. East wall, third door. Packet by hand. I didn't take a copy up to Cressida's office. A Chainman crossing inside his licence needn't, and I didn't, and I'd like the record to show that those are two separate facts.

Weirside's Ninefold has green curtains. They were drawn back, and Mrs Prowse was at the Exchange Desk with her pen already wet. Behind her the pigeonholes ran up to the ceiling in green-painted wood, one of them labelled Ardent, which is my surname and not my pigeonhole.
"Bole packet," I said, and put it down.

She turned it to the window and checked the seal, as she has checked every Bole seal since day twelve. "Untouched. We've had a good month for wax." She signed for it. Then she looked at me over her spectacles, the way people at that desk look at me. "Our Ardent came home on day seventy-nine with nothing in his pockets and his bills buttoned inside his shirt. He wrote to you that night." She tipped her pen at the stairs. "He's in the registry. He said you'd come early or not at all."

Weirside's Ardent was at the long table under the registry window with his bills laid out in rows, the way I lay out mine. He had a cup of tea at his elbow. While I watched, he read a line on one of the bills, then put sugar in the tea.
Footnote: I don't take sugar. I don't know if he used to.
He had my face. I was ready for that. I wasn't ready for how much it had been used.
"Ardent," I said. Survey custom is surnames. It saved us both a decision.
"Ardent." It was my voice, with the guard down. "You took your time."
"Six days. I can account for every one."
"I know you can. So could I." He pushed a chair out with his foot. "Footnote: I'd have taken six days too."
He says them out loud. I had been told that, and it still landed.
My letter from day thirty lay open at his elbow, the creases gone soft. "I read it on day seventy-nine," he said. "It had been in my pigeonhole since day thirty-one. Prowse kept it dusted."
"And they call you?"
"Yorath." He said it as if he had practised it, which I suppose he had. "Prowse. My father. The register. The bench on the east bank, if benches called people anything."

I put my own folder on the table, open at day nought, so that we were even. He read my first line, the one that reads false, and didn't say anything for a while. Then he turned two of his bills round so they faced me.
The first was a plain sheet, dated day nought, in pinned ink, in my handwriting, which is his. One line. My given name is Edric. It read false.
The second was a Form 9, dated day twenty-eight. Line one: My given name is Fintan. It read false too. In the margin, by the same hand, the reason, worked in the order the rule gives it.
I read the reason. I already knew it, because I'd worked it out myself in the Bole, but I hadn't known it was right.

Footnote: Lockhythe, distance twenty-nine, day sixty-one, his exit. One, hinge facts: none on the bill. Two, glare: he carried nothing Lockhythe lacked. He had learned that much by then. Three, ballast: none left. Ballast is made at home and settles at the seventh midnight. A man who stays out longer than a week crosses unballasted after that, every door, every time. Four, orphans, oldest first. The oldest thing he held that Lockhythe didn't support was a name he had received from me. A received fact keeps its first owner's age, so it counted as old as my naming. Lockhythe's Ardent is called Yorath. Nothing there agreed with Fintan. So Fintan went, and Yorath came.
"Why not sooner?" I said. "You'd been unballasted for weeks."
"Everywhere else I paid, the Ardent there was called Fintan too. The name agreed. It was safe." He shrugged. "Till Lockhythe."

I counted the false lines. I can't help it. Across six bills from day twenty-eight to day seventy-nine, eleven lines read false. Four rents and seven exits, out past anything Weirside licenses, and his ballast settling behind him at every seventh midnight like a tide going out. He could no longer whistle. A scar across his left palm, from a sluice chain at twelve, was gone, and he had a stranger's mark on his wrist instead. His first day at the Survey belonged to somebody else. Line one of the day-twenty-eight bill was the only one of the eleven that had been mine first.

Footnote: what he paid. On day nought he paid his own name for mine. At Lockhythe he paid mine away. And Lockhythe's Ardent, who never met either of us, woke on day sixty-one answering to a name he didn't choose. Somebody there calls him Fintan to his face every day. I owe him an apology. There is no form for it.

I copied the chain into my case notes in pinned ink, with my own bottle, which I can't really spare this quarter. Day nought, Weirside hall's door to the Bole: Fintan to him, Edric to me. Day sixty-one, Lockhythe's door to wherever he went next: Fintan to Lockhythe's Ardent, Yorath to him. Two swaps, two doors, three men. I drew a line under it and wrote, in the margin, with a dagger: settle from the far end in.
He watched me do it. "That's how I'd have written it," he said.
"You did write it. Your margin."
"So I did."
"Is Lockhythe standing?"
"It was when I left it." He looked at the window. "I don't know about this morning. I don't know about anything far, this morning."
Noted.
"Come now," I said. "Come alone. Bring ballast."

"Now, because I don't know how long Lockhythe has." He ticked them off on his fingers, the way I do. "Alone, because I didn't know where he'd be, and one of you is easier to keep track of than three. Bring ballast, because I came home without any, and I didn't want you doing it my way."
"You could have said so."
"In a letter? In a packet that somebody on your side was opening and reading?" He waited. "I heard about the wax."
"That was a night clerk reading about his daughter."

"I know that now. I didn't on day seventy-nine." He picked up the day-nought sheet and put it down again, square to the table edge. "It's a good name, Yorath. It's his. I'd like him to have it back. He's walking about in yours, and I'm walking about in his, and you're walking about in mine, and none of us asked."
Footnote: three men, one name each, all of them borrowed. I drew it as a diagram later. It didn't help.
"What's at the far end?" I said.
He took a while. He drank some of the tea he'd sugared.
"Since spring I've been following the cold ones," he said. "Pins that go dead all at once."
"Calder Fold. A chart in a Greyfell clerk's head. In the margin: cold by morning, not decay."
"Mine."
"In my dagger."

"Ours." He nearly smiled. "Out there I met a man. He was kind to me. He was old. He knew the routes the way you know your own stairs in the dark. He wrote me one further than Weirside will license anybody and signed under it as my leader. I brought it home and entered it, and went out on day twenty-eight to meet him where he said."
I took out my notebook and turned to day forty-two, where I had copied the mark from Weirside's register. A small ring, open at the top. A stroke across the gap.
He put his finger on it. "That's his."
"You crossed with him."

"For a while." He turned his cup a quarter turn on the saucer. "Where we'd been, the doors went cold after. Not while I was there. After. So I stopped going with him and went after him instead. By the dead ones. Outward, as far as Lockhythe." He was quiet. "At the last door we stood at together I asked him straight. Was it him closing them. He said yes. He said it kindly. He didn't say how, and he didn't say why."
"Where is he now?"
"There isn't a branch where he isn't."
"That isn't a measurement."
"No," Yorath said. "It's what it was like."
I had a Chainman's order, written in my Form 9 folder in pinned ink, six days old. When someone knows more than they should, ask their name. Write it down.
"What's his name?"
"I asked him that too." He held my eye. "He didn't answer. He wasn't rude about it. He just didn't."

I wrote the report there, at his table, on a Weirside sheet. Time, place, informant. Then the line for the party. Standing Order 12.5: a party whose name is not known shall be entered under a working name, to be struck when the name is known. A working name describes what the party does.
I wrote: the Arborist.
Footnote: an arborist is a man you pay to take branches off a tree. I didn't write down that anybody paid him. I don't know that anybody did.
Yorath read it upside down across the table. "Fits," he said.
"There's more," I said. "Isn't there."
"One thing. A message, for you." He started gathering his bills into their rows. "I'll give it you at the door."
"Why at the door?"
"Because then you'll have to take it home," he said, "instead of staying here to argue with it."
"Go and see him," Yorath said, after noon. "He knows you're here. Mother's at the chandler's till four."
"I'll be gone by four."
Footnote: I know why. It isn't going in the report.

The way to Sluice Row goes along the east bank, past the weir. At home, on that bank, there is a stone slab with four names cut into it, and I walk past it twice a day. Here there is a bench. Plain oak, gone silver, nobody's name on it. A woman was eating an apple on it and watching the sluice gates, which were shut and dry and doing their job.
I didn't sit on it. I counted the planks. Seven. There is nothing else on this bank to count.
Number 11, Sluice Row. Green door, a brass knocker shaped like a fish. He opened it before I knocked. Tall, grey at the temples, a pencil behind his ear. My jaw, or I have his.
"Kettle's on," he said, and stood aside.

The kitchen was as I'd left it on day forty-two: the dresser of blue plates, the tide chart pencilled on the wall by the window, one line for every day of the month. He didn't call me anything. He poured the tea, and he didn't put sugar in mine, and he didn't ask. He looked at the chart instead and said the river was high for the month, which it was. I'd seen the gauge on the way.
On day forty-two I had sat at this table and lied for an afternoon, and he had let me. I had carried the question home and back again.
"Why did you let me?" I said. "Pretend."
He sat down across from me. "Because he asked me to. Before he went far. He said, 'If a man with my face comes, let him have the afternoon. Don't make him pay for it.' So I didn't."
"He knew I'd come."

"He knew you'd come. I didn't know you'd come twice." He turned his cup on its saucer a quarter turn. I had watched his son do the same thing three hours earlier. "He tells me he was Fintan for a while. I remember naming him Yorath. I'd swear to it on the weir."

Footnote: after a swap, the branch rewrites the fact's own footprint, and that includes other people's memories of it. My father remembers choosing a name that was chosen for somebody else in a branch he's never seen. He isn't lying. The rule did the choosing for him.
I had decided on the walk over, between the registry and the bench, that I would say one true thing. One. I had not decided which.

"In the Bole," I said, "you went down to the sluice gates on the weir night. You drowned there. There's a slab on the east bank with four names on it, and yours is third. My mother raised me on her own."
He was standing by then. I don't know when he had stood up. He took it standing, one hand flat on the dresser, between two blue plates. He didn't sit down again, and he didn't ask me to stop.
"Is she well?" he said.
"She's well."
He nodded, slowly, as if he were measuring the river and the number was the one he'd expected.
Then he looked at me properly, the way he looks at the water.
"Edric," he said.
On purpose. I could tell it was on purpose, because he waited after it to see what I would do.
"My son tells me I chose it," he said. "Somebody ought to use it who means it."
I didn't correct him.
Footnote: I'd like it on the record that I didn't want to.

His voice is low, and it goes hoarse at the ends of things. I have had it since day forty-two. Facts acquired inside a branch are never taken there, so this door can't take it. It's every other door I worry about.
I was out of Sluice Row by a quarter to four.
Yorath was waiting at the end of the street, sitting on a bollard with his hands in his pockets. He didn't ask me anything until we were past the weir.
"Did he call you it?"
"Yes."
"Good," he said, and that was all, and we walked the rest of the way to the Hall saying nothing in exactly the same rhythm.
At dusk Mrs Prowse gave me Weirside's packet for the Bole, since I was the post today, and signed me out.
"You're going to try it anyway," Yorath said. He had his day-nought sheet in his hand. Mine was in my folder. "You know it won't work."
"I know the rule says it won't work."
"Reverse order. Lockhythe first, then here."
"Yes."
"And Lockhythe is twenty-nine hinges out. You're licensed to two. I'm licensed to four."
"Yes."
"So nobody in Weirside's hall can lead a crew to where your name is."
"Not this year," I said.
Footnote: Surveyor Third reaches four. Second, eight. First, sixteen. Cartographer, thirty-two. I did that sum on the stairs and didn't like the answer. I did it again on the landing. Same answer.
"Then why?"
"Cressida says nobody has ever shown her a bill for the mirror rule," I said. "I want to be able to show somebody a bill for this one. And a rule you haven't tried is a rumour."
Yorath looked at Mrs Prowse. "Footnote: he's always like this."
"So are you," said Mrs Prowse.

The swap was charged on day nought at this door, Weirside hall's, on the route to the Bole's east wall, third door. Eighty-six days set. Thirty is the minimum. Two bills in pinned ink. Two men, both willing, nobody paid. Every clause I could find was met except one, and I wanted to watch that one fail with my own eyes.

Yorath stood in Weirside's door and read the route to the Bole. The stone warmed. Weirside's opening, his reading; mine had gone at dawn. He stepped back out of the frame to let me by, and through it I could see the Bole's threshold room, empty, the lamps just lit.
"Nine," I said. Brisk's orders.

"Eight." I stepped through and stood on the Bole's flagstones with Weirside's packet under my arm, and read my bill in the doorway's light, because Standing Order 9.1 says to read it at the threshold. Four lines. All true.

Footnote: Least Agreement on my exit. No hinge facts. Nothing in my kit that Weirside lacks. One ballast, fresh, of a kind Weirside hadn't had from me. It went. My bill is clean. The voice was never at risk here.
"Seven." I turned round and put my hand through the open door.

Reaching through is not a crossing. Yorath took my hand on his side, in Weirside, and I held his on mine, in the Bole, and we stood like that in the frame the swap was charged to, with both our bills held up to the light in our free hands.
"Day nought," I read. "My given name is Fintan."
"Day nought," he read. "My given name is Edric."
"Six," I said. "Five."
Nothing.
The word stayed what it has been since day nought: a word. The line on my bill read false. His did too. I could feel his pulse in his thumb, and it was mine, slightly faster.

Footnote: he doesn't hold it. Settlement reverses one swap between the two people who made it, and Yorath no longer has what I'd be taking back. Lockhythe's Ardent has it. So it's a chain. Lockhythe to Weirside first, at the Lockhythe door where it was charged, with Lockhythe's Ardent willing. Then Weirside to the Bole, here. In reverse order, and before anybody cuts Lockhythe.
There. Now somebody has a bill for it.
"Four. Three."
Yorath let go first. He didn't step back from the frame.
"Two," I said. That is breath eight, counting up, which is how the rule counts.
He leaned into the doorway, as close as you can come without crossing, and said it fast and low.
"He knew your name. Both of them. He said to tell you you've already met him."
